```{r setup, include = FALSE}
                      fig.height = 4.5)
```

```{r load}
library(mirt)
library(irtident)
```

## A 3PL example

Convergence and a positive-definite information matrix do not establish
precise estimation of every parameter. mirt provides the information-matrix
condition number as one summary of numerical conditioning:

```{r fit}
dat <- expand.table(LSAT7)
fit <- mirt(dat, 1, itemtype = "3PL", SE = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
extract.mirt(fit, "secondordertest")
extract.mirt(fit, "condnum")
```

A large condition number motivates closer inspection, although its magnitude
depends on the parameter scale. irtident adds diagnostics by item and parameter.

## Combined diagnostics

```{r diagnose}
set.seed(1)
dx <- id_diagnose(fit, n_starts = 8)
dx
```

Four of the five items have a guessing parameter at its lower bound: for
them the data are consistent with a 2PL item. Item 2's guessing parameter
is estimated at about 0.3, but it is associated
with the intercept, and the data cannot rule out `g = 0`.

The diagnosis combines three pieces of evidence, described below.

## 1. Local diagnostics: where does the uncertainty come from?

`id_local()` splits each parameter's sampling variance into three factors:

$$SE_j^2 = SE_{cond,j}^2 \times VIF^{within}_j \times VIF^{between}_j$$

* $SE_{cond,j}$: the standard error if every other parameter were known
  (how much information the data carry about this parameter alone);
* $VIF^{within}_j$: inflation from not knowing the other parameters *of the
  same item*;
* $VIF^{between}_j$: inflation from not knowing the parameters of *other
  items* and of the latent distribution.

```{r local}
loc <- dx$local
p <- loc$params[loc$params$item == "Item.2",
                c("param", "value", "se", "se_cond", "vif_within", "vif_between")]
p
```

For item 2, the within-item variance inflation factors for `g` and `d` are
about 20 in the reference run. This corresponds to a standard-error multiplier
of about $\sqrt{20}$, not 20. The local standard errors for `g` are on the
logit scale. The correlation-matrix diagnostic also reports parameter
combinations associated with small eigenvalues:

```{r directions}
loc$directions
```

### Guessing parameters in easy items

Consider a 3PL test with `a = 1.5` and `g = 0.2` for every item and a range
of difficulties. The following code evaluates expected (Fisher) information
at the generating values. The information depends on those values and N;
the simulated data provide the mirt object used for the calculation.

```{r sim}
set.seed(2026)
n_items <- 12
b <- seq(-2.5, 2.5, length.out = n_items)
sim <- simdata(matrix(1.5, n_items), matrix(-1.5 * b), N = 3000,
               itemtype = "3PL", guess = 0.2)
pv <- mirt(sim, 1, itemtype = "3PL", pars = "values")
pv$value[pv$name == "a1"] <- 1.5
pv$value[pv$name == "d"] <- -1.5 * b
pv$value[pv$name == "g"] <- 0.2
at_truth <- mirt(sim, 1, itemtype = "3PL", pars = pv, TOL = NaN,
                 verbose = FALSE)
loc_truth <- id_local(at_truth, SE.type = "Fisher")
g_rows <- loc_truth$params[loc_truth$params$name == "g", ]
round(data.frame(b = b, se = g_rows$se, se_cond = g_rows$se_cond,
                 vif_within = g_rows$vif_within), 2)
```

```{r sim-plot, fig.height = 4}
plot(b, g_rows$se, log = "y", pch = 19, type = "b",
     xlab = "item difficulty b", ylab = "SE of logit(g), log scale",
     main = "Precision of guessing estimates by item difficulty (N = 3000)")
```

The lower asymptote is most evident at low ability relative to item
difficulty. For easy items, few respondents occupy that region. In this
example, easy items have less conditional information about `g` and greater
within-item confounding with the intercept.

## 2. Profile likelihood: is the interval closed?

`id_profile()` fixes a parameter at a grid of values, re-estimates
everything else, and records the deviance. A parameter is practically
identified when its profile likelihood interval is closed on both sides
(Raue et al., 2009).

```{r profile}
dx$profile
```

```{r profile-plot, fig.height = 5}
plot(dx, params = c("Item.1:g", "Item.2:g", "Item.4:g", "Item.2:a1"))
```

For `Item.2:g` the Wald interval excludes 0, but the profile interval
reaches it. The difference indicates that a local quadratic approximation
does not describe the full profile well. For `Item.1:g`, the profile does
not cross the cutoff over the evaluated range from 0 to 0.5. These intervals
use an asymptotic chi-squared cutoff; coverage can differ from the nominal
level at boundaries and under weak identification.

## 3. Multiple starting values

`id_multistart()` refits from random starting values and clusters the
solutions. Clusters with the same log-likelihood but different parameter
values can indicate weak identification or distinct modes. Clusters with
lower log-likelihood suggest optimisation problems. Convergence needs to
be checked before treating either group as optima. For example:

```{r multistart}
fit4 <- mirt(dat, 1, itemtype = "4PL", verbose = FALSE)
set.seed(2)
ms <- id_multistart(fit4, n_starts = 6)
ms
```

Starts that hit the iteration limit remain in the comparison. Slow convergence
can accompany weak identification, but is not sufficient evidence of it.

## 4. Parameter precision across sample sizes

`id_samplesize()` simulates from the fitted model at several sample sizes,
refits, and compares repeated-estimate SD with the SEs reported by mirt. These additional
fits can be expensive, so the simulation is separate from `id_diagnose()`:

```{r samplesize, eval = FALSE}
set.seed(1)
ss <- id_samplesize(fit, params = c("Item.2:g", "Item.2:a1"),
                    N = c(1000, 2000, 4000, 8000), reps = 20)
ss
plot(ss)
```

For each parameter and N, the summary reports:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `current` | Estimate from the original fitted model |
| `mean` | Mean of the repeated estimates |
| `sd` | SD of the repeated estimates |
| `mirt_se` | Root mean squared mirt SE, `sqrt(mean(SE^2))` |
| `n_used` | Replications used for the mean, SD and mirt SE |
| `success` | Successful fits divided by all attempted fits |
| `conv` | Converged fits divided by all attempted fits |
| `se_failure` | Fraction of converged successful fits without a usable estimate/SE pair |

The mean, SD and mirt SE use the same replications: converged fits with a
finite estimate and a finite, positive SE for that parameter. An SE
calculation failure does not discard the raw estimate, but excludes that
replication from these paired summaries. The SD is unavailable with fewer
than two usable replications; `se_failure` is unavailable if none converged.
Raw estimates and reporting-scale SEs are retained in `ss$estimates` and
`ss$standard_errors` with matching N and replication numbers.

`plot(ss)` compares SD and mirt SE across N. Their decline shows how much
precision a larger sample may provide under the generating model. Differences
between the two curves suggest that mirt's SEs and the simulated variability
are not in close agreement. Inspect `n_used`, convergence and SE failure
alongside the curves: excluding difficult fits can make precision look better.
The 20 replications in this example illustrate the procedure and may leave
substantial simulation variability.

For `g` and `u`, both curves use the probability scale. The logit SE from
mirt is converted with the delta method, `p * (1 - p) * SE_logit`. At exact
probability boundaries the SE is marked unavailable; near a boundary this
approximation can still be unreliable. SEs are evaluated at the converged
estimates without further optimisation, using the same fitting arguments.
Use `SE.type` to choose a different mirt SE method.

The function does not calculate bias or RMSE, set a precision cutoff, or
automatically choose a sample size. The `truth` argument retains its name
for compatibility and specifies the generating model; it defaults to `fit`.
These results describe that simulation scenario, not known population values.

## Running in parallel

All diagnostics that refit the model accept `parallel = TRUE` and then use
`future.apply` with whatever `future::plan()` is active:

```{r parallel, eval = FALSE}
future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 4)
dx <- id_diagnose(fit, parallel = TRUE)
```

## Scope of this version

* Unidimensional, single-group models from `mirt::mirt()`.
* Itemtypes `Rasch`, `2PL`, `3PL`, `3PLu`, `4PL` and `graded`.
* No equality constraints.

## References

Chalmers, R. P. (2012). mirt: A multidimensional item response theory
package for the R environment. *Journal of Statistical Software, 48*(6),
1-29.

Raue, A., Kreutz, C., Maiwald, T., Bachmann, J., Schilling, M.,
Klingmuller, U., & Timmer, J. (2009). Structural and practical
identifiability analysis of partially observed dynamical models by
exploiting the profile likelihood. *Bioinformatics, 25*(15), 1923-1929.
